Eirini Katsidoniotaki, Themistoklis P. Sapsis∗
Department of Mechanical Engineering,
Massachusetts Institute of Technology,

March 12, 2026
Abstract
Predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems remains a fundamental challenge, as
such events are rare, intermittent, and arise from transient dynamical mechanisms that are difficult to infer from
limited observations. Accordingly, real-time forecasting calls for precursors that encode the mechanisms driving
extremes, rather than relying solely on statistical associations. We propose a fully data-driven framework for long-
lead prediction of extreme events that constructs interpretable, mechanism-aware precursors by explicitly tracking
transient instabilities preceding event onset. The approach leverages a reduced-order formulation to compute
finite-time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE)–like precursors directly from state snapshots, without requiring knowledge
of the governing equations. To avoid the prohibitive computational cost of classical FTLE computation, instability
growth is evaluated in an adaptively evolving low-dimensional subspace spanned by Optimal Time-Dependent
(OTD) modes, enabling efficient identification of transiently amplifying directions. These precursors are then pro-
vided as input to a Transformer-based model, enabling forecast of extreme event observables. We demonstrate the
framework on Kolmogorov flow, a canonical model of intermittent turbulence. The results show that explicitly
encoding transient instability mechanisms substantially extends practical prediction horizons compared to baseline
observable-based approaches.
keywords: Extreme events prediction; Dynamical precursors; Time-series forecasting;
1 Introduction
Extreme events are rare yet high-impact episodes, associated with abrupt changes in the state and dynamics of a
system, that arise across a variety of natural and engineering systems—including oceanic rogue waves [19], extreme
weather [23], shocks in power grids [44], and sudden market drawdowns [16], just to mention a few examples. They
often lead to severe humanitarian, environmental, and financial consequences, motivating the development of
real-time forecasting tools that enable timely mitigation.
To formalize this notion, an extreme event may be defined as a high-amplitude excursion of a system response
that markedly exceeds the typical fluctuations generated by the background dynamics [22, 43]. In time series,
such excursions appear as intermittent bursts: short-lived peaks separated by long intervals of typical behavior.
In practice, extremes are specified with respect to an observable—a scalar quantity of interest derived from the
system state, such as wave crest height in ocean dynamics, or portfolio losses in financial markets. An event is
deemed extreme when the observable attains values in the far tail of its empirical (or stationary) distribution, and
thus occurs with very low probability under nominal conditions.
While this definition provides a clear criterion for identifying extremes, it does not by itself make them predictable:
extreme excursions may develop rapidly and often exhibit weak or ambiguous precursory signatures. As a result,
real-time prediction hinges on identifying measurablediagnostic quantitiesthat characterize the evolving system
and exhibit consistent, detectable changes prior to event onset. We refer to such diagnostics asprecursorsof
extremes. For a precursor to be practically useful, it must robustly discriminate impending extremes from typical
fluctuations, yielding low false-positive and false-negative rates. In this context, even partial understanding of

the dynamics that underlie the extreme events and trigger their formation can guide the discovery and design of
reliable precursors that facilitate the data-driven prediction of extremes [8,22,43].
In the context of extreme events associated with special type of dynamics, such as instabilities, special emphasis
should be given to mechanism-linked features rather than purely statistical correlations. For example, in un-
steady aerodynamic flows, pressure-based precursors—often constructed to isolate event-relevant dynamics (e.g.,
via spectral or wavelet filtering) and informed by sparse-sensing measurements—have been coupled with sequential
time-series models to improve prediction of intermittent force excursions [8,29,40]. In turbulent flows with external
forcing, mechanism-based precursors of extreme dissipation bursts have been identified by linking burst onset to
characteristic nonlinear interactions among Fourier modes and associated depletion of low-wavenumber energy,
while the underlying trigger of this energy exchange remains unresolved [12,21]. A dynamical–statistical approach
was proposed for wall-bounded turbulence that identifies precursors of extreme dissipation events by computing
an attractor-consistent critical state via finite-time energy-growth optimization and using its alignment with the
instantaneous flow as an interpretable early-warning indicator. Recent work [48] has further shown that dissipa-
tion bursts of comparable magnitude can exhibit markedly different predictability depending on their underlying
dynamical route, underscoring the need for mechanism-linked, pathway-discriminative precursors. Similarly, in dif-
ferent domains such as medicine, instability-informed scalars, such as data-driven Lyapunov-exponent estimates,
have been used in deep-learning models for event detection and forecasting in physiological time series [47].
On the other hand, we have purely data-driven precursors, where predictive signatures of upcoming extremes are
learned directly from data and statistical associations [15,26]. In the same spirit, relevant efforts have increasingly
leveraged deep learning methods to predict extreme events directly from time-series data, including recurrent ar-
chitectures, such as reservoir computing [3,18,37,39] and LSTM-based models [50]. To improve performance recent
works proposed extreme-event-tailored loss functions [41] and optimal sampling approaches [10] to emphasize rare
events during training. In addition, attention-based sequence models have been proposed to improve performance
by explicitly separating “normal” from “extreme” regimes [2]. In this purely data-driven paradigm, attribution
and explainability methods can be used to extract the input patterns most responsible for a model’s predictions
(e.g., for heatwave forecasting), yielding “machine-view” precursors that support knowledge discovery [51]. While
powerful, these precursors are typically association-based, they rely on a large number of extremes for training,
whereas dynamics-based precursors are constructed to explicitly quantify the underlying dynamical pathways to
extremes.
In this study, we focus on high-dimensional systems in which extremes are generated byinternal transient insta-
bilitiesand we build dynamical precursors that encode the responsible dynamics. More specifically, we utilize a
geometric viewpoint, where the system evolves primarily on a background attractor where the trajectories lie most
of the time. Extreme events occur when the system enters localized regions of this attractor where the dynamics be-
come strongly nonlinear and exhibit finite-time instabilities [43]. In this case the state is transiently repelled from
the main attractor, causing a rapid amplification of the observable that appears as an intermittent burst in the time
series [12,21,33]. Our goal is to formulate dynamic precursors by encoding the local unstable dynamics associated
with these transient events. This is done by relying on the observation that, even in high- or infinite-dimensional
systems, the emergence of extreme events is typically dominated by a small number of transiently-positive Lya-
punov exponents, i.e. by a small number of effective modes. These modes are hard to capture with traditional
spectral decomposition methods —such as dynamic mode decomposition [45] and Koopman-mode analysis [32]—
due to their essentially transient character.
To address this challenge we employ the Optimal Time-Dependent (OTD) framework [6], in a fully data-driven
formulation. OTD modes define an adaptive, trajectory-dependent low-dimensional subspace that continuously
aligns with the directions of maximal transient growth, i.e. directions associated with the largest finite-time
Lyapunov exponents (FTLE), and therefore with the finite-time instabilities that precede extreme excursions [7].
The key idea is to discover features that directly track the finite-time instability direction responsible for extreme-
event growth and to use those to synthesize a precursor of an upcoming extreme event. This is achieved by
computing the FTLE in the reduced-order subspace spanned by the OTD modes. Previous work [20] relied on
purely OTD-based precursors capturing local-in-time transient amplification, whereas our FTLE-based approach
encodes instability growth accumulated over a finite horizon. A key remaining challenge is to translate mechanistic,
trajectory-based instability diagnostics, in this case FTLE, into reliable forecasts of event occurrence from time-
series observations. Recent work has shown that the predictive skill for rare extremes depends not only on the use
of dynamically informative, mechanism-linked features but also on their integration with appropriate deep-learning
architectures to improve forecasting performance and extend lead times [5]. In our case, we address this step by
employing a Transformer-based architecture that exploits temporal context to forecast extreme-event occurrence
over a prescribed lead time, using the FTLE obtained in earlier times.
We demonstrate the method on a prototype high-dimensional turbulent system —the Kolmogorov flow— in which
extremes appear as intermittent bursts of the total energy dissipation rate, showing that the proposed framework
extends substantially the effective prediction horizon relative to baseline precursors while maintaining computa-
tional efficiency, thereby enabling practical early warning in settings where extreme events pose significant risk.

3 Extreme Event Precursors
We now formulate a fully data-driven framework for the real-time prediction of extreme events in chaotic, high-
dimensional dynamical systems. The framework consists of two components. The first component provides a
methodology for computing reduced-order FTLEs using just data, i.e the sequence of snapshots{u(t k)}N
k=0. The
second component is the predictive, where the leading FTLE, ˆΓ1, computed from system observations up to timet,
provides dynamical information that is mapped directly to the predicted value of the observable, ˆz, at a prescribed
lead timet+τ. If the predicted value exceeds the threshold condition ˆz(t+τ)≥z∗, we have have identified an
extreme event. In this section we discuss in detail the various steps involved (Figure 2).

3.4 Performance measures for precursors of extreme events
To evaluate the predictive skill of the proposed precursors, we adopt several binary classification metrics [26].
Specifically, each prediction outcome is categorized as one of four outcomes: atrue positive(TP) when an extreme

6 Conclusions
We have introduced a fully data-driven framework for long-horizon prediction of extreme events in high-dimensional
chaotic dynamical systems, with emphasis on extremes generated by internal transient instabilities. The key idea
is to move beyond purely statistical indicators and instead construct interpretable, dynamics-informed precursors
that encode the dynamical pathways responsible for extreme-event formation.
We have relied on the concept of FTLEs which provide a natural description of the transient instability growth that
precedes extreme events; however, since their classical computation is prohibitively expensive in high-dimensional
systems, we adopt a reduced-order, data-driven approach based on OTD modes to compute FTLEs efficiently. Since
the governing equations are unavailable and only state observations are assumed, the system dynamics required for
OTD evolution are approximated directly from data and used solely to infer the local variational behavior. The
resulting leading FTLE provides a physically grounded measure of finite-time instability growth, capturing the
dynamical buildup preceding extreme excursions. We demonstrate how these FTLE-based precursors, computed
using information available up to the present time, can be integrated with a Transformer-based architecture to
enable long-horizon prediction of extreme events.
The developed architecture is applied to the two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, where extremes manifest as inter-
mittent bursts of energy dissipation. Across multiple evaluation criteria—including binary classification metrics
and statistical consistency measures—the FTLE-based approach consistently achieves higher predictive skill and
robustness, particularly at forecast horizons beyond those previously attainable with Fourier-based precursors.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel data-driven framework for predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems. The core challenge addressed is the rarity and intermittency of these events, which are driven by transient dynamical mechanisms that are difficult to infer from limited observations.

The proposed framework aims to construct interpretable, mechanism-aware precursors by explicitly tracking transient instabilities preceding event onset. Key points covered include:

*   **Problem Definition:** Extreme events are defined as rare, high-amplitude excursions of a system's observable that significantly exceed typical fluctuations. Real-time prediction requires precursors that encode underlying dynamical mechanisms, not just statistical associations.
*   **Mechanism-Based Precursors:** The approach emphasizes the importance of understanding the dynamics that trigger extreme events, particularly transient instabilities.
*   **Optimal Time-Dependent (OTD) Modes:** To efficiently identify transiently amplifying directions without knowing the governing equations, the framework leverages OTD modes. These modes form an adaptively evolving low-dimensional subspace that aligns with directions of maximal transient growth, akin to finite-time Lyapunov exponents (FTLEs).
*   **Reduced-Order FTLE Computation:** The computational cost of traditional FTLE calculation is prohibitive. The document details a method to compute FTLEs within the reduced-order subspace spanned by OTD modes, enabling efficient identification of instability growth.
*   **Transformer-Based Prediction Model:** The computed FTLEs are used as input to a Transformer-based deep learning model. This model learns to forecast extreme event observables by exploiting temporal context and the information encoded in the FTLEs.
*   **Data-Driven Approach:** The entire framework is designed to be equation-agnostic, relying solely on state snapshots from time-series data. This involves data-driven modeling of system dynamics and Jacobian-vector products.
*   **Output-Weighted Loss Function:** A specialized loss function is employed during training to emphasize the accurate prediction of rare, high-magnitude events by weighting samples inversely proportional to their probability density.
*   **Performance Evaluation:** The document outlines several metrics for evaluating the predictive skill of the precursors, including F1-score, Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC), maximum adjusted area under the curve, extreme event count, and quantification of tail statistics.
*   **Prototype Model (Kolmogorov Flow):** The framework is demonstrated on Kolmogorov flow, a canonical model of intermittent turbulence. The energy dissipation rate is used as the observable, and extreme events are defined as significant bursts in this quantity. The results show that explicitly encoding transient instability mechanisms substantially extends practical prediction horizons compared to baseline observable-based approaches.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.summary:
This partial document introduces a novel data-driven framework for predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems. The core challenge addressed is the rarity and intermittency of these events, which are driven by transient dynamical mechanisms difficult to infer from limited data. The proposed approach focuses on constructing interpretable, mechanism-aware precursors by explicitly tracking transient instabilities that precede event onset.

Key points covered include:

*   **Problem Definition:** Extreme events are rare, high-impact episodes characterized by abrupt changes and high-amplitude excursions in system observables, often leading to severe consequences. Real-time prediction requires precursors that encode underlying dynamical mechanisms, not just statistical associations.
*   **Limitations of Existing Approaches:**
    *   **Statistical Associations:** Purely data-driven methods learn from statistical correlations but may lack explainability and require extensive data.
    *   **Mechanism-Based (Traditional):** While some mechanism-based precursors exist (e.g., linking to nonlinear interactions or critical states), they can be computationally expensive or may not fully capture transient dynamics.
*   **Proposed Framework:**
    *   **Focus on Transient Instabilities:** The framework leverages the idea that extreme events in many systems arise from transient instabilities within localized regions of the system's attractor.
    *   **Finite-Time Lyapunov Exponent (FTLE)-like Precursors:** The approach computes precursors that encode instability growth directly from state snapshots, without needing the governing equations.
    *   **Reduced-Order Formulation with Optimal Time-Dependent (OTD) Modes:** To overcome the computational cost of classical FTLE computation, the framework uses OTD modes. These modes define an adaptively evolving low-dimensional subspace that aligns with directions of maximal transient growth (associated with FTLEs), enabling efficient identification of transiently amplifying directions.
    *   **Transformer-Based Prediction Model:** The computed FTLE precursors are fed into a Transformer-based deep learning model. This model leverages temporal context to forecast extreme event observables over a prescribed lead time.
*   **Demonstration and Results:** The framework is demonstrated on Kolmogorov flow, a canonical model of intermittent turbulence. The results indicate that explicitly encoding transient instability mechanisms significantly extends practical prediction horizons compared to baseline observable-based approaches, while maintaining computational efficiency.
*   **Keywords:** Extreme events prediction, Dynamical precursors, Time-series forecasting.

nodes.title: Preliminaries and Background
nodes.summary:
This partial document introduces the problem setup for analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems, focusing on the characterization and prediction of "extreme events." It defines a general nonlinear dynamical system and its state space. The core concepts discussed are:

*   **Problem Setup:** Modeling a general nonlinear dynamical system governed by an ordinary or partial differential equation.
*   **Flow Map:** Describing the evolution of the system state over time.
*   **Extreme Events:** Defining extreme events as rare, intermittent excursions of an observable to unusually large values, often occurring away from typical fluctuations on a chaotic attractor.
*   **Variational Equation and Local Stability:** Linearizing the system dynamics to study the evolution of infinitesimal perturbations, which helps understand local, finite-time stability properties relevant to extreme events.
*   **Lyapunov Spectrum Limitations:** Explaining that while Lyapunov exponents characterize long-time asymptotic stability and chaotic behavior, they do not capture transient instabilities crucial for predicting extreme events.

structure.title: Conclusions
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a data-driven framework for predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems, focusing on those generated by internal transient instabilities. The core idea is to use interpretable, dynamics-informed precursors, specifically Finite-Time Lyapunov Exponents (FTLEs), to encode the dynamical pathways leading to extreme events. Since direct computation of FTLEs is expensive, a reduced-order, data-driven approach using Optimal Transport Decomposition (OTD) modes is employed for efficient computation.

The framework integrates these FTLE-based precursors with a Transformer-based architecture for long-horizon prediction. The performance of this FTLE-based approach is compared against a widely used Fourier-based precursor in the context of two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, where extreme events are characterized by bursts in energy dissipation.

Key findings include:
- The FTLE-based predictor consistently outperforms the Fourier-mode-based model in predicting extreme energy dissipation events, especially at longer forecast horizons.
- This advantage is most pronounced for prediction horizons up to $\tau=10$, where the FTLE-based approach maintains near-optimal performance metrics like F1-score and AUC.
- Even at longer horizons ($\tau=15$), the FTLE-based predictor retains a substantial performance advantage, accurately reproducing dissipation dynamics and capturing the timing and magnitude of large-amplitude events, albeit with a modest increase in false positives.
- The FTLE-based forecasts preserve better agreement in the probability density functions of energy dissipation, particularly in the high-dissipation regime, up to $\tau \approx 10-12$, whereas Fourier-based forecasts show significant tail attenuation.
- The document details the methodology for approximating system dynamics from data and the architecture of the Transformer-based time-series forecasting model.

The proposed framework is applicable to a broad range of high-dimensional systems where extremes arise from transient instabilities, including turbulent flows and geophysical systems.

nodes.title: Evaluate reconstruction accuracy
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the training of a neural network model for simulating Kolmogorov flow dynamics. Key points include:

*   **Model Architecture (ResCNN):** A ResCNN architecture is used as a baseline, noting its computational efficiency and focus on local feature extraction, while acknowledging its limitations in capturing global or multiscale interactions.
*   **Loss Function for Chaotic Systems:** The document highlights the inadequacy of standard L2 (mean-square error) loss for chaotic systems like Kolmogorov flow, which exhibit multiscale behavior. L2 loss tends to over-smooth predictions and neglect crucial fine-scale details (gradients, oscillations) that encode physical quantities like energy dissipation and vorticity.
*   **Sobolev Training:** To address the limitations of L2 loss, the document introduces and adopts Sobolev training. This method incorporates higher-order spatial derivatives into the loss function, penalizing discrepancies not only in field values but also in their gradients, thus improving the representation of fine-scale physical features. The Sobolev norm of order k (Hk) is defined and explained in both real and Fourier space, emphasizing how higher orders (k=1 for velocity gradients, k=2 for vorticity and dissipation) capture increasingly fine-scale information. The specific loss function used is the H2 norm of the discrepancy between predicted and reference velocity time derivatives.
*   **Reconstruction Accuracy Evaluation:** The accuracy of the learned map (ˆF) is assessed by comparing predicted time derivatives with reference values using three neural architectures: FNO, ResUNet++, and ResCNN. Errors are quantified using Sobolev norms of order k=0, 1, and 2 (H0, H1, H2) to provide a scale-aware measure of performance.
*   **Comparison of Architectures:** Results (Table 1) show that the FNO achieves the lowest errors across all Sobolev orders, indicating superior accuracy. ResUNet++ performs comparably but with higher errors, while ResCNN exhibits significantly larger errors, reflecting its limited capacity for multiscale and nonlocal interactions.
*   **Vorticity and Energy Spectra Analysis:** Visualizations (Figure 9) of vorticity derivatives and energy spectra further support these findings. FNO and ResUNet++ accurately reproduce dominant structures and temporal evolution, while ResCNN underestimates gradients. Energy spectra show that FNO and ResUNet++ closely match reference solutions, with deviations at the highest dissipative scales.
*   **Data-driven OTD Modes:** The document also discusses the computation and evaluation of data-driven Optimal Transport Decomposition (OTD) modes. Comparisons of the curl of these modes (Figure 10) between equation-based and data-driven predictions show that the data-driven approach accurately reproduces the spatial organization and temporal evolution of leading modes, with minor localized discrepancies in higher-order modes. Energy spectra for OTD modes also show close agreement.
